pharm: Selectively blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors peripherally on vagal nerve terminals and centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, preventing the emetic reflex.
quick: 8 mg PO; 24 mg single dose for highly emetogenic chemo
May take with or without food
Inconsistent data; use only if clearly needed
Limited data; likely compatible, monitor infant
summary: Ondansetron is a selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist used to prevent nausea and vomiting from chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and surgery. It is dose-limited in severe hepatic impairment and carries a risk of dose-dependent QT prolongation.
indications: Prevention of nausea/vomiting with highly emetogenic chemotherapy (cisplatin >=50 mg/m2)
Prevention of nausea/vomiting with initial and repeat courses of moderately emetogenic chemotherapy
Prevention of nausea/vomiting from radiotherapy (total body irradiation, single high-dose or daily abdominal fractions)
Prevention of postoperative nausea and/or vomiting

dosage.n: For single-day highly emetogenic chemo including cisplatin >=50 mg/m2

dosage.d: 8 mg, then 8 mg 8 hours later; then 8 mg twice daily (q12h)
dosage.t: 30 min before chemo; continue 1-2 days after completion

dosage.d: Do not exceed 8 mg total daily dose

admin: Administer first dose 30 minutes before chemotherapy (1-2 hours before radiotherapy)
May be given with or without food
Orally disintegrating tablets: place on tongue and allow to dissolve, do not push through foil
Do not exceed 8 mg/day in severe hepatic impairment
Assess QT risk factors before use
moa: Ondansetron is a selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy release serotonin from enterochromaffin cells of the small intestine; serotonin activates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, triggering the vomiting reflex. Ondansetron blocks these receptors to prevent emesis.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to ondansetron or formulation components
Concomitant use of apomorphine (risk of profound hypotension and loss of consciousness)
monitor: ECG in patients with QT risk factors

preg: Epidemiological studies report inconsistent findings on major birth defects, with methodological limitations precluding conclusions. Postmarketing data have not identified a risk of miscarriage or adverse maternal outcomes. Use only if clearly needed.
lact: Limited human data. Ondansetron is present in animal milk. Consider development/health benefits of breastfeeding alongside maternal clinical need; monitor infant.
renal: No dosage adjustment required in renal impairment.
hepatic: In severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh >=10), clearance is markedly reduced; do not exceed a total daily dose of 8 mg.

moderate: Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin) may reduce ondansetron levels
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.

emergency: Signs of serotonin syndrome (agitation, hyperthermia, rigidity)

monitoring: ECG in patients with congenital long QT, electrolyte abnormalities, CHF, or on QT-prolonging drugs
counsel: Report fast/irregular heartbeat, fainting, or dizziness
Report agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor (possible serotonin syndrome)
Do not push orally disintegrating tablets through the foil
Inform clinician of all medications, especially heart and antidepressant drugs
pk: Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light
pearls: Single 24 mg oral dose is the standard for highly emetogenic chemotherapy
QT prolongation is dose-dependent; avoid 32 mg single IV dose
Cap at 8 mg/day in severe hepatic impairment
missed: If used as scheduled prophylaxis and a dose is missed, take when remembered unless near the next dose. Do not double up.
overdose: No specific antidote. Reported effects include hypotension, vasovagal episodes, transient blindness, severe constipation, and QT prolongation. Manage with supportive care and ECG monitoring.
